# Pull requests

A pull request is read by someone who was not there. Everything below exists
so that they can decide without asking you a question.

Commits inside it follow `kx-commit`; the code follows `kx-standards`; the
words follow `kx-style`. This file is about the request itself.

## One intent

A pull request does one thing, named in its title. A reviewer reading two
things at once reviews the first properly and skims the second, and the bug
is always in the second.

- A fix and the refactor that made it possible are two requests, the
  refactor first. The fix then reads as a diff of ten lines instead of two
  hundred.
- Formatting, renames and dependency bumps travel alone. Mixed into a
  feature they hide it.
- Something noticed on the way is an issue (`kx-issue`) or the next request,
  never a passenger in this one.

Size follows from that. There is no line limit, but a request that cannot be
read in one sitting is usually two.

## The title

The subject line of the commit it would squash to, in the form `kx-commit`
gives: `<type>(<scope>): <subject>`, imperative, lower case, in English. A
title that fits the changelog is a title a reviewer can predict the diff from.

## The body

Written for two readers: the reviewer now, and whoever runs `git log` on it in
a year. Neither has your context.

```markdown
## Why

The problem, or the reason the change is worth making, in the words of
whoever will notice it. A link to the issue is not a replacement.

## What

What changed, at the level of decisions rather than files. Say what was
rejected and why when there was a real alternative.

## How to verify

The command, its expected output, and where to click when there is a UI.
Verbatim, so the reviewer runs it rather than reads it.

## Not in this PR

What was deliberately left out, so nobody reviews for its absence.
```

Leave out a section that has nothing to say; never leave a heading over
nothing. A UI change carries a screenshot or a recording; "looks the same" is
a claim, a screenshot is evidence.

## Before opening it

In this order, because each one changes what the next one finds:

1. **Read your own diff**, whole, as the reviewer will. Every request has one
   thing in it that its author would have flagged in somebody else's.
2. **Tests pass locally**, and the ones you added fail without the change.
3. **Nothing unrelated moved.** A formatter run over a file you touched for
   one line has turned a one-line review into a four-hundred-line one.
4. **No secret, no credential, no `.env` value.** `.env.op` references are
   fine; anything that would work if pasted is not.
5. **Rebased on the base branch**, so the diff is yours and only yours.

Then:

```bash
gh pr create --title "<type>(<scope>): <subject>" --body-file <the body> [--draft]
```

Draft while it is not ready to merge. A draft says "look if you want"; a
request says "this can go in", and a request that cannot wastes the reviewer's
first read.

## Responding to review

A review comment is a claim about the code. Check it against the code before
doing anything about it, the same way `kx-issue` says to open the file before
filing.

- **It is right** → do it, push, and reply with what changed and the commit.
- **It is wrong** → say so, with the evidence — the line, the test, the
  behaviour it would break — and do not do it. A change made because someone
  asked, against what the code needs, is a bug with two authors.
- **It is unclear** → ask one precise question. Guessing at what a reviewer
  meant and implementing the guess costs two rounds; asking costs one.

Never reply "done" alone. Reply with what was done and how to see it. Never
resolve a thread you did not open; the reviewer resolves what satisfied them.

Reply in English, for the same reason commits and issues are: the thread is
read later by people who were not in the conversation.

## Watching the review — only when asked

**Never start this on your own.** Watching a request is a session that acts
on somebody else's words; the user says when that is wanted, and for which
request. Asked to "watch the PR", "atender los comentarios" or the like, do
this. Otherwise, the section does not apply.

The script lives beside this file. It talks to GitHub through `gh` so that
you do not: one call waits for the next comment, one call closes it.

```bash
S=$(find .claude/skills .agents/skills .opencode/skills \
  -path '*/kx-pull-request/scripts/pr-comments.mjs' -type f -print -quit 2>/dev/null)
test -n "$S" || { echo "KX pull-request script not found" >&2; exit 1; }

node $S status [--pr <n>]                 # the request, what is pending, what was answered, the rate limit
node $S wait   [--pr <n>] [--timeout <s>] # block until one is pending; react 👀; print it
node $S done   --id <id> --reply <file>   # post the reply, remove the 👀
```

`--pr` defaults to the request of the current branch.

**Start with `status`, whenever you start.** The script keeps nothing of its
own: a comment is *in progress* when it carries our 👀 and *handled* when our
reply is under it, both read from GitHub every time. So a session that
begins after a crash, on another machine or a week later sees the same
picture as the one that stopped, and `wait` hands back the comment that was
in progress before anything new. Tell the user what `status` says before
waiting: how many are pending, whether one was left half-done.

It recovers on its own from what ends by itself: a rate limit is waited out
until it resets, a network failure is retried with a growing pause, and
both are said on stderr. What does not end by itself, it says and stops:

| Exit | Means | You do |
|---|---|---|
| 3 | `--timeout` (default 1800s) passed with nothing pending | ask the user whether to keep waiting |
| 4 | the request was merged or closed | stop; there is nothing to watch |
| 5 | `gh` is not signed in | tell the user; `gh auth login` is theirs to run |
| 6 | `done` hit a rate limit before replying | run the same `done` again once it resets |

`done` is safe to repeat: a reply already posted is not posted twice, and a
👀 already gone is not looked for. A run that died between the two finishes
by running it again.

Only three kinds of comment count, by their first word:

| Starts with | It is | You do |
|---|---|---|
| `change:` | a change the reviewer wants | check it, then implement or refuse with the reason |
| `refactor:` | a restructuring, behaviour unchanged | check it, then do it with the tests proving nothing moved, or refuse |
| `doubt:` | a question | answer with evidence — file and line, a command and its output |

Anything else is left alone; the script never shows it to you.

The loop, one comment at a time:

1. `wait`. The comment arrives as JSON: `kind`, `body`, `author`, `path` and
   `line` for a comment on the diff, `url`.
2. Read the code it talks about. **Then decide** — the same three outcomes as
   any review comment above. The reviewer wrote one line; you have the file,
   the tests and `kx-standards`. Being asked is not a reason.
3. Do the work, if there is work: a commit per `kx-commit`, pushed to the
   request's branch, tests run first.
4. Write the reply to a file and `done`. The reply says what was done and the
   commit, or what was found and why not, or the answer and where the
   evidence is. Under a paragraph unless the evidence needs more.
5. `wait` again. Stop when the user says so, or on a timeout they do not want
   to extend.

The 👀 is the reviewer's signal that the comment is being looked at, and its
removal that a reply is there. `done` handles both; do not add reactions of
your own.

A comment that asks for something `kx-standards` forbids, or that would
break a test, gets a refusal with the reason and no code. A comment you do
not understand gets a question, not a guess. If the user is present, a
refusal is worth a sentence to them too.
